6.5

THE IDEA

A working film composer opens a Kontakt library called Ethno World 6, loads the duduk, and hears something that will not sit in a real cue: no round robins, weak legato, one dynamic. So they buy a second library, then a third. On VI-Control they trade prices ($240 for a Sonica Koto, $119 for a Premier Sound Factory Koto, $799 for Impact Soundworks' Complete World Bundle, down from $1,612) and complain that older libraries from ten years ago sound better than new ones because someone took 'Extra Care' per sample. Meanwhile Splice bought Spitfire Audio for $50M in April 2025 and in October launched Splice INSTRUMENT at $12.99/mo, bundling every Spitfire Originals sound. AI floods streaming (Deezer says 20K AI tracks upload daily, 18% of all uploads), and working composers reach for sounds no model can fake.

The idea is a boutique sample label that records one rare instrument at a time, deeply, in Kontakt. Mobile team, real player, real room, every articulation and round robin. One instrument every six to eight weeks, sold direct at $79 to $199, bundled at $499 to $799 after a dozen ship. Not a royalty split to the instrument owner (the market runs on flat royalty-free licensing, so the owner gets a flat session fee, sometimes with sync backend). A category-creation play in a niche where search is dead but the watering holes are loud.

WHY NOW

Splice paid $50M for Spitfire in April 2025, then bundled it into a $13/mo plugin in October

Two things broke open in 2025 that were not true in 2024. First, Splice acquired Spitfire Audio in April 2025 for a reported $50 million and, in October, launched Splice INSTRUMENT: a $12.99 per month plugin that bundles the full Spitfire Originals collection plus 1,200 multi-sampled presets. Spitfire's free LABS series was folded in and shut down as a standalone. The 'common ground' sample library, the pianos, strings, and pads that boutique developers used to charge $79 to $249 for, is now a Netflix subscription with 10 million producers already on the platform. A small developer cannot beat that price. What Splice does not have, and cannot cheaply record, is the long tail: a specific hurdy gurdy from a specific maker, a Bulgarian duduk played by the person who knows it, a museum piece with one working copy in the world.

Second, AI music crossed a tipping point. Deezer disclosed that 20,000 AI-generated tracks were uploaded to its platform every day in 2025, or 18% of all uploads. SlopTracker put the Spotify figure at 28%. Suno reached about 100 million users and raised at a $2.45 billion valuation. Universal and Warner signed AI licensing deals with Suno and Udio in October and November 2025. Working film, TV, game, and library composers now compete against a wave of generic AI cues. Their defense is the opposite move: authenticated, human-recorded, one-of-a-kind sounds that no model was trained on and no $13 subscription owns. Field recording gear reached the price to support this: a Zoom H1essential with 32-bit float runs about €80, a Zoom H5 handles pro captures, and Sound Devices MixPre kits cover the top end. A two-person mobile team can now record an instrument in a day for a few hundred dollars of gear amortized across a catalog.

THE WEDGE

Exclusive rights to instruments the incumbents (Spitfire, Native Instruments, Orchestral Tools, Impact Soundworks) have not sampled: regional folk, handmade one-offs, historical/museum pieces. Depth in a corner the majors ignore because the TAM per instrument is too small for them.

The incumbent to beat: Sonic Zest

PROOF & SIGNALS

Impact Soundworks, one of the boutique developers competing in this exact niche, states on its product pages that it is "TRUSTED BY 495,000+ MUSICIANS, COMPOSERS, AND HOBBYISTS", giving a direct proxy for the size of the buyer base for boutique Kontakt libraries.

IMPACT SOUNDWORKS

The global music sample library market was valued at $1.8B in 2025 and is projected to reach $4.1B by 2034 at 9.5% CAGR, with 30M+ active DAW users worldwide in 2025 (up from 18M in 2020).

DATAINTELO MUSIC SAMPLEPLACE MARKET REPORT

YouTube content demand for this exact niche is strong: Dom Sigalas' "20 Ethnic Libraries every Producer and Film Composer should know about" has 168,008 views; Sample Library Review's Ethno World 6 review has 97,264 views; Impact Soundworks' free Heritage Percussion walkthrough has 68,848 views. Producers discover these libraries through content, not search.

YOUTUBE

The music sample market is built on royalty-free licensing: producers explicitly love these libraries because there is no need for royalty payments or publishing splits to use the samples. The dominant marketplaces (Splice, Loopmasters, Tracklib, Sample Focus, Looperman) all license to the buyer flat, then pay the contributor from their own margin, not from the buyer's downstream music revenue. Any royalty split with the instrument owner is a cost paid by the developer out of its own sale, not by the composer.

Sonic Zest

Soniccouture

(UK boutique, since ~2005) is the flagship boutique developer of rare/unusual Kontakt instruments.

Spitfire Audio

The market-leading orchestral sample library developer (founded 2007, London, partnerships with Hans Zimmer and Abbey Road).

Orchestral Tools

(Berlin) is the premium orchestral incumbent with its own SINE player.

Splice

, the largest sample/loop marketplace for producers, launched Splice INSTRUMENT at $12.99/month that includes the entire Spitfire Audio Originals collection (20+ virtual instruments, $600+ of sounds).

Pianobook

(founded 2018 by Spitfire Audio co-founder Christian Henson) is the free peer-to-peer alternative and the DIY status quo: 500+ contributors have shared 1,000+ virtual instruments for Kontakt and the free Decent Sampler player.

's Ethno World 6 is the incumbent all-in-one world/ethnic Kontakt library: 264 instruments in 620 patches, 24.7 GB, 23,559 samples, built over 16 years by film composer Marcel Barsotti with 70+ musicians.

VI-Control forum · Salohcin894

“I think what I'm craving is some off color winds, like a solo recorder or odd horns. I know that organic samples has the majestic horn, but I tend to write more understated things. That being said it's what, 2 euros?”

THE VERDICT

Should you build this?

REASONS TO BUILD

Working composers publicly name the exact instruments they cannot find well-sampled (hurdy gurdy, sitar, Armenian/Bulgarian/Turkish duduks, mandolin, mandola, banjo, zither) and complain that Ethno World and UVI World Suite are too shallow to sit in a real cue.
The market already pays real money for single-instrument depth: Sonica Koto at $240, Premier Sound Factory Koto at $119, Impact Soundworks Complete World Bundle at $799 down from $1,612, Soniccouture and Sonic Zest running healthy boutique catalogs for 20 and 10+ years.
Two 2025 events sharpen the wedge: Splice bought Spitfire for $50M in April and bundled Originals into $12.99/mo INSTRUMENT in October (kills the low end but validates the premium single-instrument shelf), while AI music hit 18% of Deezer uploads daily (drives working composers toward sounds AI cannot fake).
AI agents handle Kontakt scripting and Decent Sampler ports, so a single founder with audio-engineering ears and VI-Control credibility can ship twelve libraries in eighteen months without a technical co-founder or funding.

REASONS TO NOT BUILD

Search demand for the concept is essentially zero (rare instrument VST, folk instrument VST, ethnic sample library combined add to under 1,000 monthly searches); this is category-creation through forums and YouTube walkthroughs, not a growth-hack story.
Year one grosses roughly $16K on one library and 150 units; the catalog only compounds in year three. Any founder who needs income in six months will quit before it works.
Splice INSTRUMENT at $12.99/mo owns 10 million producers and could add a 'Rare Instruments' subscription pack that collapses the $29 to $79 shelf overnight, forcing every survivor into the $149+ zone.
The market has settled on flat royalty-free licensing (Tracklib, every named boutique), so the brief's owner-royalty wedge is a founder invention that pays out of thin margin; the real differentiation has to be sample depth and access, both of which take years to prove.

Search will not save this business. Category demand is real (Spitfire Audio pulls 8,100 searches a month, Kontakt library 590 a month), but the concept-level queries (rare instrument VST, folk instrument VST, ethnic sample library) add to well under 1,000 monthly searches combined. WHY NOW

Splice paid $50M for Spitfire in April 2025, then bundled it into a $13/mo plugin in October

Two things broke open in 2025 that were not true in 2024. First, Splice acquired Spitfire Audio in April 2025 for a reported $50 million and, in October, launched Splice INSTRUMENT: a $12.99 per month plugin that bundles the full Spitfire Originals collection plus 1,200 multi-sampled presets. Spitfire's free LABS series was folded in and shut down as a standalone. The 'common ground' sample library, the pianos, strings, and pads that boutique developers used to charge $79 to $249 for, is now a Netflix subscription with 10 million producers already on the platform. A small developer cannot beat that price. What Splice does not have, and cannot cheaply record, is the long tail: a specific hurdy gurdy from a specific maker, a Bulgarian duduk played by the person who knows it, a museum piece with one working copy in the world.

Second, AI music crossed a tipping point. Deezer disclosed that 20,000 AI-generated tracks were uploaded to its platform every day in 2025, or 18% of all uploads. SlopTracker put the Spotify figure at 28%. Suno reached about 100 million users and raised at a $2.45 billion valuation. Universal and Warner signed AI licensing deals with Suno and Udio in October and November 2025. Working film, TV, game, and library composers now compete against a wave of generic AI cues. Their defense is the opposite move: authenticated, human-recorded, one-of-a-kind sounds that no model was trained on and no $13 subscription owns. Field recording gear reached the price to support this: a Zoom H1essential with 32-bit float runs about €80, a Zoom H5 handles pro captures, and Sound Devices MixPre kits cover the top end. A two-person mobile team can now record an instrument in a day for a few hundred dollars of gear amortized across a catalog.

First up.

Search will not save this business. Category demand is real (Spitfire Audio pulls 8,100 searches a month, Kontakt library 590 a month), but the concept-level queries (rare instrument VST, folk instrument VST, ethnic sample library) add to well under 1,000 monthly searches combined. Google Trends for Kontakt library shows a declining pattern over the last twelve months. Nobody types the problem statement into a search bar. The first 100 buyers come from three watering holes where working composers already talk about this problem: VI-Control's Sample Talk sub-forum, YouTube walkthroughs by composer channels like Dom Sigalas (his 20 Ethnic Libraries video pulled 168K views), and the front page of Loot Audio when a new library ships.
